newsitem.title: GERMANY: Commerzbank says ends tax dispute with authorities.
newsitem.headline: Commerzbank says ends tax dispute with authorities.

text.p: Germany's Commerzbank AG said on Monday it had reached agreement in its long-standing dispute with German finance officials over tax repayments.

The bank, Germany's third largest, also said a separate probe by prosecutors into bank executives' activities related to the tax dispute was continuing, but dismissed talk that changes were planned on its supervisory board.
"The Frankfurt finance authority and Commerzbank have now reached an agreement over bank tax payments for the years from 1984 to 1994," Commerzbank said in a statement.
On the basis of a government audit, the bank would make payments at levels that were "within the parameters of tax reserves set aside for this year," Commerzbank said.
The remaining reserves would be dissolved and included in 1997 accounts.

Commerzbank was ordered to pay several hundred million marks to cover back-tax for the 1984 to 1994 period after a raid on its premises early last year, but had been disputing the size of the repayment.
The raid also sparked a probe by prosecutors into the actions of senior executives at the bank amid suspicions of corporate tax evasion.

Invesigators have said they were looking into the valuation of items on Commerzbank's balance sheet, particularly losses booked at group level for U.S. subsidiaries which they say had already been written off in the U.S.
Kohlhaussen himself is being investigated in relation to his involvement in the signing of tax receipts during the period in question.
Commerzbank repeated its assertion that the probe into suspected corporate tax evasion was unfounded.
As a result, talk in the German media that there would be a need for a reshuffle in Commerzbank's supervisory board "had no basis in fact."
